The epaulette surgeonfish Acanthurus nigricauda attains a maximum body size that has been recorded at 45.3 centimeters [Li = 45.3 centimeters] in total length, a value consistent with the modest asymptotic dimensions typical of many grazing acanthurids inhabiting Indo-Pacific reef flats. Hatchlings emerge from their transparent, pelagic eggs at a remarkably small size, with the wet weight at birth estimated at approximately 0.00018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00018 grams], reflecting the minute yolk reserves available to the lecithotrophic larva during the initial days following chorion rupture. The fertilized ova, which are released during broadcast spawning events, drift within the planktonic realm before hatching, and the yolk-sac larva must rely entirely on its endogenous nutritional stores until the mouth opens and the exotrophic transition begins. Field surveys of juvenile recruitment in the central Great Barrier Reef indicate that the pelagic larval duration may extend for several weeks, although precise demarcation of this period remains under investigation. The species exhibits a typical teleost growth trajectory, with rapid increases in both length and mass occurring during the first year of benthic life as individuals establish territories on shallow patch reefs and commence grazing on filamentous algae.

Sexual maturation in Acanthurus nigricauda is closely tied to the attainment of a specific body size, with the total length at puberty documented at 18.4 centimeters [Lp = 18.4 centimeters]. At this point, the wet weight at puberty is approximately 126 grams [Wwp = approximately 126 grams], a value that may vary slightly among local populations depending on food availability and intensity of intraspecific competition. This transition from the juvenile stage to the reproductively viable adult involves the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, triggering vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. Gonadal recrudescence becomes evident as the fish approach this critical length threshold, and histological sections of the ovaries reveal the first wave of developing oocytes. The body mass at maturation represents roughly seven percent of the ultimate wet weight, which in fully grown adults can reach up to 1,800 grams [Wwi = up to 1,800 grams], a figure derived from the length-weight relationship established for this species. This allometric scaling highlights the substantial somatic investment required before the onset of reproductive activity, a pattern common among iteroparous reef fishes that delay breeding until a size refuge from predation is secured.

The maximum recorded longevity of Acanthurus nigricauda in the wild is approximately 45 years [am = approximately 45 years], a lifespan that is notably extended among the Acanthuridae and suggests a slow life-history pace relative to many other surgeonfishes of comparable maximum size at a temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C]. This estimate, which is based on otolith increment analyses conducted at a stable water temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], implies that individuals may survive for more than four decades on the reef, provided they avoid predation and habitat degradation. Such a prolonged lifespan is characteristic of species that invest in structural growth early and then maintain minimal adult mortality through crypsis and diurnal sheltering behavior. The oldest individuals sampled from populations in the Coral Sea have shown well-defined annual rings that corroborate the slow growth rates inferred from length-frequency distributions. Senescence appears to be gradual, with reproductively active adults continuing to spawn into their fourth decade, although fecundity may decline slightly in the oldest age classes. This extensive post-pubertal period, combined with the species protracted maturation, yields a life cycle in which reproductive opportunities are distributed across many years.

Under the stable thermal regime of a typical coral reef habitat at 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], a mature female Acanthurus nigricauda releases an estimated approximately 1,750 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 1,750 eggs per day], a reproductive rate inferred from the species' characteristic high fecundity as a member of the Acanthuridae. Spawning aggregations form at dusk along the outer reef slope during the summer months, with gravid females releasing their pelagic oocytes into the water column in synchronized bouts. This high daily fecundity is characteristic of a group-synchronous ovary organization, where clutches of developing oocytes mature sequentially across the breeding season. The estimated 640,000 eggs produced annually per female represent a substantial investment in offspring, though individual egg size remains small, reflecting the planktonic larval strategy that relies on high fecundity to offset heavy mortality during the pelagic phase. Field observations confirm that females may spawn multiple times over the course of a single season, and the nutritional condition of the adult prior to spawning strongly influences the total number of oocytes that undergo vitellogenesis. This reproductive pattern reflects an adaptive trade-off between egg size and egg number, optimized for dispersal in a variable oceanographic environment.

A comparison of life-history traits across the genus Acanthurus reveals that A. nigricauda occupies an intermediate position along the slow-fast continuum, with its age at first reproduction and maximum size falling between those of smaller, short-lived species like Acanthurus triostegus and the larger, more long-lived Acanthurus leucosternon. The ability of this surgeonfish to persist for up to 45 years [am = up to 45 years] allows for multiple reproductive seasons, spreading the risk of recruitment failure across decades at a temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C]. Despite its modest size at hatching of roughly 0.00018 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.00018 grams], the species compensates through a high fecundity and a long reproductive lifespan. Reaching a total length of 18.4 centimeters [Lp = 18.4 centimeters] and a body mass of 126 grams [Wwp = 126 grams] signals the onset of puberty, a size threshold reached relatively late in life that defers reproduction until a survival advantage is secured. The ultimate adult length of 45.3 centimeters [Li = 45.3 centimeters] balances maneuverability on the reef with the ability to defend feeding territories against conspecific competitors.
